title: Data Governance
html:
1Core Definition and Goals

Definition: Data Governance (DG) is the exercise of authority, control, and shared decision-making (planning, monitoring, and enforcement) over the management of data assets.

Key distinction: DG ensures data is managed properly — it does not directly execute data management. It represents an inherent separation of duty between oversight and execution (like an auditor vs. accountant).

3 Goals of Data Governance

  1. Enable an organization to manage its data as an asset
  2. Define, approve, communicate, and implement principles, policies, procedures, metrics, tools, and responsibilities for data management
  3. Monitor and guide policy compliance, data usage, and management activities

DG vs. IT Governance

Data Governance IT Governance (COBIT)
Focus Management of data as an asset IT investments, application & project portfolio
Scope Data assets exclusively Hardware, software, technical architecture
Alignment Business data strategy IT strategies with enterprise goals
Note

Sarbanes-Oxley spans corporate governance, IT governance, and data governance.

2Business Drivers

Most common initial driver: regulatory compliance (financial services, healthcare).
Other entry points: MDM programs, major data quality problems.

DG drivers focus on:

Reducing Risk:

  • General risk management (E-Discovery, legal/regulatory)
  • Data security (availability, usability, integrity, consistency, auditability)
  • Privacy (PII control, compliance monitoring)

Improving Processes:

  • Regulatory compliance
  • Data quality improvement
  • Metadata management / Business Glossary
  • Efficiency in development (SDLC, technical debt management)
  • Vendor management (cloud, external data, outsourcing)

3DG Program Requirements

A successful DG program must be:

Requirement Meaning
Sustainable Not a project with an end; requires ongoing organizational commitment and change management
Embedded Incorporated into software development, analytics, MDM, and risk management processes
Measured Has positive financial impact; must demonstrate this through metrics and baselines

46 DG Principles

  1. Leadership and Strategy — Visionary, committed leadership; data strategy driven by enterprise business strategy
  2. Business-driven — DG is a business program that governs IT decisions about data as much as business interaction with data
  3. Shared Responsibility — Shared between business data stewards and technical data management professionals across all KAs
  4. Multi-layered — Occurs at both enterprise and local levels (and levels in between)
  5. Framework-based — Operating framework defines accountabilities and interactions across functional areas
  6. Principle-based — Guiding principles are the foundation of DG activities and especially of DG policy

5Data Governance Organization

Legislative / Judicial / Executive Analogy

  • Legislative-like: Defining policies, standards, Enterprise Data Architecture
  • Judicial-like: Issue management and escalation
  • Executive: Protecting and serving, administrative responsibilities

5 DG Bodies / Committees

Body Description
Data Governance Steering Committee Highest authority; cross-functional senior executives; oversight, support, and funding; releases funding as recommended by DGC and CDO
Data Governance Council (DGC) Manages DG initiatives, issues, and escalations; executive composition per operating model
Data Governance Office (DGO) Ongoing focus on enterprise-level data definitions and standards across all DAMA-DMBOK KAs; coordinating roles (stewards/custodians, data owners)
Data Stewardship Teams Communities of interest focused on specific subject areas or projects; business and technical stewards, data analysts
Local Data Governance Committee Divisional/departmental councils in large organizations; smaller organizations should avoid such complexity

6Three Operating Model Types

Model Description
Centralized One DG organization oversees all activities in all subject areas
Replicated Same DG operating model and standards adopted by each business unit independently
Federated One DG organization coordinates with multiple Business Units to maintain consistent definitions and standards

7Data Stewardship

Definition: Data Stewardship is the most common label to describe accountability and responsibility for data and processes that ensure effective control and use of data assets.

Key stewardship activities:

  • Creating and managing core Metadata (Business Glossary)
  • Documenting rules and standards (business rules, data quality rules)
  • Managing data quality issues (identification and resolution)
  • Executing operational DG activities (day-to-day, project-by-project)

"The best Data Stewards are often found, not made" — DAMA-DMBOK 1st edition. (However, stewards can also be trained.)

7 Types of Data Stewards

Type Role
Chief Data Steward Chairs DG bodies in lieu of CDO; may act as CDO in virtual/distributed DG; may be Executive Sponsor
Executive Data Steward Senior managers who serve on the Data Governance Council
Enterprise Data Steward Oversight of a data domain across business functions
Business Data Steward Business professionals (SMEs); accountable for a subset of data; defines and controls data with stakeholders
Data Owner A business Data Steward with approval authority for decisions about data within their domain
Technical Data Steward IT professionals in one of the KAs (DBA, BI Specialist, DQ Analyst, Metadata Admin, etc.)
Coordinating Data Steward Leads/represents teams of business and technical stewards; especially important in large organizations

8Data Policies

Definition: Directives that codify principles and management intent into fundamental rules governing creation, acquisition, integrity, security, quality, and use of data.

  • Policies describe the 'what' (what to do / not do)
  • Standards and procedures describe 'how' to do data governance
  • Policies should be few, brief, and directly stated
  • Policies are global in nature

9Data Asset Valuation

Data only brings value when used. Value = economic benefit of use > cost of acquiring/storing + risk management.

Ways to measure data value:

Method Description
Replacement cost Cost to recover lost data after disaster or breach
Market value Value as a business asset at time of merger/acquisition
Identified opportunities Income potential from BI insights, transactions, or selling data
Selling data Packaging data as a product or selling insights
Risk cost Penalties, remediation costs from absence/presence of wrong data, or incorrect data

10Generally Accepted Information Principles (GAIP)

Translated from Generally Accepted Accounting Principles — 10 principles:

Principle Core Idea
Accountability Identify individuals ultimately accountable for all data/content types
Asset Data/content are assets; must be managed, secured, and accounted for like financial assets
Audit Accuracy of data/content subject to periodic audit by an independent body
Due Diligence Known risk must be reported; possible risk must be confirmed
Going Concern Data is critical to ongoing business operations — not a temporary by-product
Level of Valuation Value data at the level that makes the most sense or is easiest to measure
Liability Financial liability connected to regulatory and ethical misuse or mismanagement
Quality Meaning, accuracy, and lifecycle of data can affect the financial status of the organization
Risk Risk associated with data must be formally recognized as a liability or through cost management
Value Value exists in data based on usage, marketability, and contribution to goodwill (balance sheet)

11Activities (17 Total, in 4 Groups)

Group 1: Define Data Governance for the Organization (Planning)

# Activity
2.1 Define DG for the Organization
2.2 Perform Readiness Assessment
2.3 Perform Discovery and Business Alignment
2.4 Develop Organizational Touchpoints

Group 2: Define the DG Strategy (Planning)

# Activity
2.5 Develop Data Governance Strategy
2.6 Define the DG Operating Framework
2.7 Develop Goals, Principles, and Policies
2.8 Underwrite Data Management Projects
2.9 Engage Change Management
2.10 Engage in Issue Management
2.11 Assess Regulatory Compliance Requirements

Group 3: Implement Data Governance (Operations)

# Activity
2.12 Implement Data Governance
2.13 Sponsor Data Standards and Procedures
2.14 Develop a Business Glossary
2.15 Coordinate with Architecture Groups
2.16 Sponsor Data Asset Valuation

Group 4: Embed Data Governance (Control/Operations)

# Activity
2.17 Embed Data Governance

12Key Activities Detail

Readiness Assessment — 4 Types

  1. Data management maturity — Current DM capabilities and capacity
  2. Capacity to change — Organization's ability to change behaviors; identifies resistance points
  3. Collaborative readiness — Ability to collaborate in data management/use (stewardship is inherently collaborative)
  4. Business alignment — How well data uses align with business strategy

DG Strategy Deliverables (4)

  1. Charter — Business drivers, vision, mission, principles, readiness assessment, success criteria
  2. Operating framework and accountabilities — Structure and responsibility for DG activities
  3. Implementation roadmap — Timeframes for policies, glossary, architecture, asset valuation, standards
  4. Plan for operational success — Target state of sustainable DG activities

OCM/ADKAR — 5 Areas for Measuring Change Effects

  1. Awareness of the need to change
  2. Desire to participate and support the change
  3. Knowledge about how to change
  4. Ability to implement new skills and behaviors
  5. Reinforcement to keep the change in place

Issue Management — 8 Issue Types

  1. Authority (decision rights)
  2. Change management escalations
  3. Compliance
  4. Conflicts (policies, procedures, rules, definitions, standards, ownership)
  5. Conformance
  6. Contracts (data sharing, cloud, buying/selling data)
  7. Data security and identity (privacy, breach)
  8. Data quality

Issue Escalation Path

Data Governance Steering Committee    → <5%  (Strategic)
Data Governance Council               → <20% (Strategic/Tactical)
Business Unit Data Governance
Data Stewardship Teams                → 80–85% of conflicts resolved here (Tactical/Operational)

Business Glossary — 4 Objectives

  1. Enable common understanding of core business concepts and terminology
  2. Reduce risk of data misuse due to inconsistent understanding
  3. Improve alignment between technology assets and business organization
  4. Maximize search capability and enable access to documented institutional knowledge

A business glossary is NOT merely a list of terms. Each term includes: synonyms, metrics, lineage, business rules, responsible steward.

Regulatory Compliance — Key Regulations

Regulation Scope
BCBS 239 / Basel II EU banking: risk data aggregation and reporting; liquidity reporting since 2006
CPG 235 (APRA) Australian banking/insurance: data risk management throughout lifecycle
PCI-DSS Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards
Solvency II EU insurance (similar to Basel II for banks)
GASB / FASB US accounting standards impacting information asset management
Privacy laws Local, sovereign, and international laws

13CDO Organizational Touchpoints

The CDO influences four key touchpoints:

  1. Procurement & Contracts — Standard contract language for DaaS, cloud, outsourcing, content licensing
  2. Budget & Funding — Prevent duplicate efforts, optimize acquired data assets
  3. Regulatory Compliance — Monitor and track new/potential regulatory impacts
  4. SDLC / Development Framework — Identify control points for enterprise policies and standards in development lifecycles

14Tools

Tool Purpose
Online Presence / Websites Central hub for DG strategy, policies, stewardship roles, news, training, issue procedures
Business Glossary Houses agreed-upon definitions, linked to data; many standalone or embedded tools available
Workflow Tools Manage processes like new policy implementation; connect processes to documents
Document Management Manage policies and procedures
DG Scorecards Automated metrics collection; reported to DGC and Steering Committees

15Metrics — 3 Categories

Value

  • Contributions to business objectives
  • Reduction of risk
  • Improved efficiency in operations

Effectiveness

  • Achievement of goals and objectives
  • Extent stewards are using relevant tools
  • Effectiveness of communication
  • Effectiveness of education/training
  • Speed of change adoption

Sustainability

  • Performance of policies and processes (are they working?)
  • Conformance to standards and procedures (are staff following guidance?)

16Context Diagram Summary

Component Examples
Inputs Business/IT/Data Strategies, Org Policies, Business Culture Assessment, Data Maturity Assessment, IT Practices, Regulatory Requirements
Deliverables DG Strategy, Data Strategy, Roadmap, Data Principles, Policies, Operating Framework, Business Glossary, DG Scorecard, Communications Plan
Participants Steering Committees, CIO, CDO/Chief Data Stewards, Executive Data Stewards, Coordinating Data Stewards, Business Data Stewards, DG Bodies
Metrics Compliance to regulatory/internal data policies; Value; Effectiveness; Sustainability
Tools Websites, Business Glossary Tools, Workflow Tools, Document Management, DG Scorecards

17Exam Q&A (20 Questions)

Q1. How is Data Governance defined in DMBOK2? A: The exercise of authority, control, and shared decision-making (planning, monitoring, and enforcement) over the management of data assets.

Q2. What are the 3 goals of Data Governance? A: (1) Enable organization to manage data as an asset; (2) Define/approve/communicate/implement principles, policies, procedures, metrics, tools, and responsibilities; (3) Monitor and guide policy compliance, data usage, and management activities.

Q3. What is the key distinction between Data Governance and Data Management? A: DG ensures data is managed (oversight); Data Management actually manages data (execution). This is a separation of duty — similar to how an auditor sets financial rules but doesn't do the accounting.

Q4. How does Data Governance differ from IT Governance? A: DG focuses exclusively on management of data assets. IT Governance (COBIT) focuses on IT investments, application portfolio, and project portfolio — hardware, software, and technical architecture.

Q5. What are the 3 requirements for a successful DG program? A: Sustainable (ongoing, not a project), Embedded (incorporated into processes), Measured (demonstrates positive financial impact).

Q6. What are the 6 DG Principles? A: Leadership & Strategy, Business-driven, Shared Responsibility, Multi-layered, Framework-based, Principle-based.

Q7. What are the 3 DG Operating Model types? A: Centralized (one DG org for all), Replicated (same model adopted by each BU), Federated (one DG coordinates with multiple BUs).

Q8. Which DG body has the highest authority? A: The Data Governance Steering Committee — highest authority; cross-functional senior executives; responsible for oversight, support, and funding.

Q9. What percentage of data governance conflicts are resolved at the Data Stewardship Team level? A: 80–85%. Less than 20% reach the DGC, and less than 5% reach the Steering Committee.

Q10. What is a Data Owner? A: A business Data Steward who has approval authority for decisions about data within their domain.

Q11. What is the difference between Data Policies and Data Standards/Procedures? A: Policies describe the 'what' (what to do and not do); Standards and procedures describe 'how' to carry out data governance.

Q12. What are the 4 types of Readiness Assessments? A: (1) Data management maturity; (2) Capacity to change; (3) Collaborative readiness; (4) Business alignment.

Q13. What does ADKAR stand for in the context of OCM? A: Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement — the 5 areas for measuring the effects of change management.

Q14. What are the 4 objectives of a Business Glossary? A: (1) Enable common understanding of business concepts/terminology; (2) Reduce risk of data misuse; (3) Improve alignment between technology assets and business; (4) Maximize search capability and access to institutional knowledge.

Q15. Name 5 of the 10 Generally Accepted Information Principles. A: Any 5 from: Accountability, Asset, Audit, Due Diligence, Going Concern, Level of Valuation, Liability, Quality, Risk, Value.

Q16. What regulation applies to EU banking liquidity reporting (since 2006)? A: BCBS 239 / Basel II — Principles for Effective Risk Data Aggregation and risk reporting.

Q17. What is CPG 235? A: An Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) standard for managing data risk throughout its lifecycle; applies to banking and insurance entities.

Q18. What role does the Coordinating Data Steward play? A: Leads and represents teams of business and technical Data Stewards in discussions across teams and with executive Data Stewards; especially important in large organizations.

Q19. What are the 3 metric categories for DG programs? A: Value (contributions, risk reduction, efficiency), Effectiveness (goals, tools usage, communication, training, speed of adoption), Sustainability (policy performance, conformance to standards).

Q20. What does it mean for DG to be 'embedded'? A: DG activities are incorporated into development methods for software, analytics, MDM, and risk management — DG is not an add-on process.
